clarifyingQuestions: Can a path be both a file and a directory?
Should writes create parent directories or fail if parents don't exist?
followUps: Add delete with recursive directory behavior.
followUpGuide: For append, reuse `write_file` traversal but concatenate to existing file content. If the file doesn't exist, clarify whether append should create it.
For delete, decide whether deleting non-empty directories requires `recursive=True`. That choice affects safety much more than code complexity.
For tenant isolation, namespace the root by tenant ID or store tenant on every node and check it during traversal. Don't rely on path prefixes alone.
complexityAnalysis: - Let L be the input path length, d its component count, k the listed directory's child count, and B the total characters stored in names and file contents. Splitting and hashing path components costs O(L), even when dictionary lookup uses an average constant number of probes.

- Flat path map approach: normalized full-path lookup costs O(L) on average. Without a child index, listing scans n stored paths and sorts the k matching child names. Total storage includes all repeated full-path prefixes and file contents.

- Trie/tree approach: mkdir, write_file, and read_file traverse in O(L) average time. ls adds O(k log k) comparisons to sort names; comparing long names also costs character work. The tree stores O(n + B) space and path parsing uses O(L) temporary space. String assignment and return reuse immutable strings here.

- Recursive delete follow-up: visit s subtree nodes. A depth-first traversal can use O(d) call-stack space; an explicit stack of all pending children can grow to O(s). Recursive listing also pays for its output and any requested sorting.
solutionGuide: A trie-like tree is the clearest model: directory nodes own child maps and file nodes own content.
Normalize paths into components by splitting on `/` and dropping empty parts. This handles repeated slashes and trailing slashes.
return [part for part in path.split("/") if part]
